title: Memory Management and Leak Prevention
description: Understand JavaScript garbage collection, identify common memory leak patterns, and apply memory-efficient coding practices in browser applications.

data.text: JavaScript garbage collection automatically reclaims memory from objects that are no longer reachable. But automatic does not mean free: leaks still happen, and memory pressure causes slow garbage-collection pauses, tab crashes, and degraded performance on low-memory devices.

Primitives like numbers and booleans live on the stack, while objects, arrays, and functions live on the heap. The stack is fast and bounded; the heap is large but slower. Most performance problems come from how the heap is used, not the stack.

data.title: Memory Allocation in Practice
data.content: Understanding where JavaScript values are stored.

data.text: Modern engines use generational, incremental, and concurrent garbage collection. New objects go in the young generation and are collected frequently because most objects die young. Survivors are promoted to the old generation, where collection is slower but less frequent.

data.title: Generational GC Overview
data.content: How modern engines organize and collect memory.
data.code:
Generational Garbage Collection:

Young Generation (Nursery):
- New objects allocated here
- Frequent, fast minor GC
- Most objects die here (generational hypothesis)

Old Generation:
- Objects that survived young-gen GC
- Infrequent, expensive major GC
- Contains long-lived caches, closures, DOM wrappers

Scavenge (Minor GC):
- Copies live objects from young to young
- Reclaims memory by wiping the from-space
- Very fast (milliseconds)

Mark-and-Sweep (Major GC):
- Marks all reachable objects from roots
- Sweeps unmarked objects
- May require compaction to reduce fragmentation

Concurrent Marking:
- Marks reachable objects on a background thread
- Reduces main-thread pause time
- Available in modern V8

data.text: The most common leaks in web apps are accidental global references, uncleared timers, unreleased event listeners, closures capturing large objects, and detached DOM nodes kept alive by JavaScript references.

data.title: Leak Patterns and Fixes
data.content: Identify and fix common memory leaks.

data.text: Object pooling, typed arrays, and WeakMap/WeakSet caching reduce allocation pressure. For numeric-heavy workloads, typed arrays use contiguous memory and avoid boxing overhead.

data.title: Object Pool and Typed Arrays
data.content: Reduce allocation pressure in hot paths.

data.text: Use Chrome DevTools Memory panel to detect leaks. Take heap snapshots before and after an action. If the heap grows unexpectedly and retained size stays high, you likely have a leak. The Allocation Instrumentation timeline shows allocation stacks in real time.

data.title: DevTools Memory Workflow
data.content: Systematic approach to finding memory leaks.
data.code:
Memory leak investigation workflow:

1. Open DevTools > Memory
2. Select 'Heap snapshot' and click 'Take snapshot'
3. Perform the suspected leak action (open/close, add/remove)
4. Take another snapshot
5. Compare snapshots

What to look for:
- Objects with increasing 'Distance' from GC roots
- Detached DOM nodes growing between snapshots
- Closures retaining large arrays or strings
- Event listeners or timers not released

Allocation timeline:
- Record allocation over time
- Interact with the app
- Look for allocations that never get reclaimed

data.title: Browsers Enforce Memory Limits
data.text: Most browsers enforce per-tab memory limits (often 1–4 GB on desktop, much less on mobile). Exceeding these limits crashes the tab. Long-running SPAs, image galleries, and offline apps are especially prone to leaks; build cleanup routines and test navigation cycles.

terms.definition: A garbage collection strategy that divides objects into young and old generations and collects them at different frequencies.
A DOM node removed from the document but still referenced by JavaScript, preventing garbage collection.
A map that does not prevent its keys from being garbage collected, useful for metadata caches.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: JavaScript uses stack for primitives and heap for objects
Generational GC collects young objects frequently and old objects rarely
Common leaks: globals, timers, listeners, closures, detached DOM
Clear timers and listeners on unmount or cleanup
Use object pools for high-frequency allocations
Use typed arrays for numeric-heavy workloads
Use WeakMap/WeakSet for caches that should not prevent GC
Detect leaks with heap snapshots in DevTools
data.takeaway: Memory leaks are not mysterious: they are references that live too long. Audit cleanup paths, use heap snapshots regularly, and keep long-lived references minimal.
